summary: Describes common mistakes found in DNS implementations and suggests fixes for them.

plainLanguage.summary: Many people made the same mistakes building the Internet's phone book. This memo lists them so others can avoid them.

questions: what is a dns fast retransmission
why do dns resolvers need negative caching
what are common dns implementation errors
subtitle: A catalogue of recurring DNS software bugs that flooded the network with traffic, and how to fix them.

tldr.problem: Different DNS implementations interacted badly in the early 1990s and produced huge amounts of unnecessary traffic on the NSFnet backbone.
tldr.mechanism: The memo names seven common errors, shows how BIND 4.8.3 and 4.9 behaved as an example, and lists concrete fixes such as exponential back-off, retry limits and negative caching.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo, not a standard, and it was updated by RFC 9210.

today: RFC 1536 is Informational, not a standard, and it was updated by RFC 9210. It reflects the BIND versions and DNS practice of October 1993.

sections.title: Why This Memo Exists
sections.content:
The authors observed what they call an explosion of DNS traffic on the NSFnet backbone. Various DNS implementations and versions interacted and produced large amounts of unnecessary traffic. The memo documents known problems and fixes so implementers know what to watch for.

Where it applies, it points out violations of RFC 1034 and RFC 1035, and it describes the algorithms in BIND versions 4.8.3 and 4.9 as examples of good, and sometimes bad, practice.
sections.plainLanguage: Too many badly behaved programs were shouting the same questions at the network. This memo explains what they were doing wrong.

sections.title: Retransmission and Dead Servers
sections.content:
DNS usually uses UDP, so the client must decide when to ask again. Fast retransmissions happen when a client repeats a query, with the same query identifier, too soon and without backing off. A correct server discards the duplicates, but they still burden the wide-area network. The fixes are to estimate round-trip times or set a reasonably high initial time-out, to back off exponentially, and, harder to deploy, to have the server send an early acknowledgement with an expected wait time.

The Berkeley stub resolver starts at the greater of 4 seconds and 5 seconds divided by the number of servers. The full-service resolver starts at the greater of 4 seconds and twice the server's round-trip estimate and backs off to a ceiling of 45 seconds.

The related failure detection bug is that some resolvers keep querying dead servers, possibly forever. The fixes are an upper limit on retransmissions, treating silence as a very large round-trip time that decays slowly, and exponential back-off. BIND limits how often it queries a server and avoids a dead server while others in the list are alive.
sections.plainLanguage: If you ask a question and nobody answers, shouting again every second is rude. Wait a little, then a bit longer each time, and stop asking someone who is clearly not there.

sections.title: Referral Loops
sections.content:
A name server that cannot answer may chain the request to servers closer to the name, or return a list of name servers for the client to try. This can go wrong in three ways: a client that ignores the referral and asks the same server again, a client that follows too many referrals in a loop (each response seen, with a different query identifier each time), and a malicious or broken server that lists itself as the server to ask.

The fixes are an upper limit on the referral and CNAME links you will chase, watching out for self-referring servers, never passing off an authority NS record with your own name on it, and accepting iterative answers from servers that do not recurse. BIND chases at most 20 referral links and 8 canonical name translations. The memo notes that a limit could, in a rare case, cut off a very long search path.
sections.plainLanguage: If you ask for directions and each person just points to the next person, and the last one points back to the first, you walk in circles. Decide in advance when to give up.

sections.title: Empty Answers, Name Errors and Caches
sections.content:
A zero answer is an authoritative NOERROR with no records: the name exists but not with the requested type. Some resolvers expect an answer record, so they resend the query, possibly endlessly. The fix is to cap retransmissions and to read such a reply as an authoritative statement that the record type does not exist. BIND does not query a server more than 3 times.

Name error bugs involve NXDOMAIN, which means the name is bad. Some resolvers keep querying, and some applications generate NXDOMAIN answers by appending the local domain to a good name first. The memo describes how the registration of the domain edu.com with a wildcard CNAME caused trouble because of this. The recommended fixes are negative caching, treating names with dots as fully qualified first, and using search lists only when explicitly specified. A secondary server that is still loading a zone may also answer NXDOMAIN wrongly, so servers should answer only after loading all zone data.

A cache leak is repeating a query within the TTL of a record already held. The fixes are to interpret TTLs correctly and not to restrict cache sizes needlessly. A last category, format errors, covers queries that do not conform to the standards and should be fixed in the resolver.
sections.plainLanguage: If you ask for a toy a shop does not sell and the shop says so, do not keep asking. And if you already wrote the answer down, look at your notes instead of asking again.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo has a Security Considerations section, but it says only that security issues are not discussed in this memo. Its recurring concern is operational: runaway retries, loops and wrong answers cost bandwidth and server time. Its related references include RFC 1535 on a security problem in widely deployed DNS software and RFC 1537 on common DNS data file configuration errors.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo is about being a good neighbour on the network, not about locks and keys. Other documents cover those.
